e-m-forster: Edward Morgan Forster was born in London on 1 January 1879, the only child of Alice Clara Whichelo and the Welsh architect Edward Morgan Llewellyn Forster, who died of tuberculosis before his son's second birthday. From 1883 to 1893 he and his mother lived at Rooks Nest, near Stevenage, which became the model for the house in Howards End. A legacy from his great-aunt Marianne Thornton gave him enough to live on and allowed him to become a writer. At King's College, Cambridge, he joined the Apostles, a secret discussion group, and met Lytton Strachey and Leonard Woolf. He later belonged to the Bloomsbury Group.

After travelling in Greece and Italy in 1903, Forster published his first novel, Where Angels Fear to Tread, in 1905. The Longest Journey followed in 1907, A Room with a View in 1908, Howards End in 1910 and A Passage to India in 1924. His short story The Machine Stops (1909) is often viewed as the beginning of technological dystopian fiction.

He spent six months in India in 1912 and 1913, visiting his friend Syed Ross Masood, to whom he later dedicated A Passage to India. During the First World War he was a conscientious objector and served as a Chief Searcher for missing servicemen for the British Red Cross in Alexandria. In the early 1920s he returned to India as private secretary to the Maharaja of Dewas, recounted in The Hill of Devi, and on coming back to England he finished A Passage to India. In the 1930s and 1940s he was a notable broadcaster on BBC Radio.

Many of the novels examine class differences and hypocrisy, and his humanism is at the heart of his work, which often shows the pursuit of personal connection despite the restrictions of society. Howards End is a condition-of-England novel about the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes and the Basts, and A Passage to India takes as its subject relations between East and West in the later days of the British Raj. It won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize.

Maurice, a story of homosexual love, was completed in 1914 but published only in 1971, the year after his death on 7 June 1970. Forster was open about his homosexuality with close friends but not with the public. He declined a knighthood in 1949 and received the Order of Merit on his 90th birthday.
eadred: Eadred was the younger son of Edward the Elder and his third wife, Eadgifu, whom Edward married in about 919. He was born around 923, and his father died in 924. He grew up with his brother Edmund at the court of their half-brother Æthelstan, probably alongside two Continental exiles, his nephew Louis, future King of the West Franks, and Alain, future Duke of Brittany. William of Malmesbury says that Æthelstan brought the infant brothers up lovingly and gave them a share in his kingdom. Eadred became king on 26 May 946, when Edmund was killed, because Edmund's sons Eadwig and Edgar were still young children.

Like Edmund, Eadred inherited the whole English kingdom but soon lost Northumbria and had to fight to regain it. The situation was complicated by rival factions. Anlaf Sihtricson, who ruled Dublin and York at different periods, and the Norse prince Erik Bloodaxe each ruled York during the reign; Erik was the more serious threat to West Saxon power.

The York magnates, led by Archbishop Wulfstan, periodically made bids for independence by accepting Viking kings and submitted to southern rule at other times. Osulf, the Anglo-Saxon ruler of Bamburgh, supported Eadred when it served his own interest. The sequence of events is unclear because manuscripts of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle contradict each other and conflict with charters. In 954 the York magnates expelled Erik, and Eadred made Osulf the first ealdorman of the whole of Northumbria.

Eadred kept most of his brother's advisers: his mother Eadgifu, Oda, Archbishop of Canterbury, and Æthelstan, ealdorman of East Anglia, who was known as the Half-King. Dunstan, Abbot of Glastonbury, was a close friend. Eadred supported the English Benedictine Reform in its early stages, appointing Æthelwold Abbot of Abingdon, but he also made Ælfsige, a married man with a son, Bishop of Winchester. Historians disagree about how much he ruled himself. Ben Snook thinks he relied on a 'kitchen cabinet', while Ann Williams calls him an able and even energetic king hampered by ill health.

Eadred was in poor health in his last years; the eleventh-century writer Herman the Archdeacon calls him crippled in both feet. He never married and died in his early thirties on 23 November 955 at Frome in Somerset. He was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His will, one of only two surviving wills of Anglo-Saxon kings, leaves estates to the Old Minster, the New Minster and the Nunnaminster. He was succeeded by Eadwig and then by Edgar, who became king of the Mercians within two years.
eamon-de-valera: De Valera was born on 14 October 1882 in New York City, at a home for destitute orphans and abandoned children in Lenox Hill, Manhattan. His uncle took him to Ireland at the age of two, and his grandmother raised him in Bruree, County Limerick. He graduated in mathematics in 1904 and taught at Rockwell College, where a colleague gave him the nickname Dev. He joined the Irish Volunteers on 25 November 1913 and rose to commandant of the 3rd Battalion.

During the Easter Rising, which began on 24 April 1916, his forces occupied Boland's Mill in Dublin. After a week of fighting he surrendered and was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted to penal servitude for life. On 21 January 1919 Sinn Féin members formed the Dáil Éireann. De Valera escaped from Lincoln Gaol in February 1919 and replaced Cathal Brugha as head of the ministry in April.

He opposed the Anglo-Irish Treaty, signed on 6 December 1921, because it replaced the Republic with a dominion whose Governor-General represented the King. Opposition to it led to the Civil War of June 1922 to May 1923, in which the pro-Treaty forces defeated the anti-Treaty IRA, whom de Valera backed. He left Sinn Féin in 1926 and founded Fianna Fáil, which abandoned abstention from the Dáil. After the 1932 election, in which it won 72 seats, he became President of the Executive Council on 9 March.

Through the 1930s he removed features of the Free State constitution that tied Ireland to the United Kingdom, and with the Constitution of Ireland of 1937 he became Taoiseach. In April 1938 he and Neville Chamberlain signed the Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement, which ended a five-year trade war and British use of the Treaty Ports, ensuring Irish neutrality in the Second World War. He declined Churchill's offers of June 1940 and after Pearl Harbor to push for Irish unity. He lost his majority in 1948 and led the opposition until 1951, and his government fell in 1954. In 1959, aged 75, he won the presidential election and handed power to Seán Lemass. He was President until 1973.

De Valera died on 29 August 1975 at Blackrock, Dublin, aged 92, and was buried at Glasnevin after a state funeral. His beliefs evolved from militant republicanism to conservatism. The biographer Tim Pat Coogan sees his time in power as one of economic and cultural stagnation, while Diarmaid Ferriter argues that the picture of an austere and backward figure was largely manufactured in the 1960s.
early-muslim-conquests: Pre-Islamic Arabia was divided along tribal and clan lines. Both the Byzantine and Sasanian empires competed for influence there through clients, the Ghassanids for the Byzantines and the Lakhmids for the Persians, who in 602 deposed the Lakhmids to take over the defence of their southern frontier themselves. This left them exposed and overextended. The Byzantine and Sasanian wars of the 6th and 7th centuries, together with outbreaks of plague, left both empires exhausted.

According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad migrated to Yathrib, later called Medina, in 622 and established the first Islamic state there. By 630 he and his followers had conquered Mecca. He died in 632, and his successor, the first caliph Abu Bakr, united the Arabian Peninsula after the Ridda Wars.

Syria was the first province taken from the Byzantines. Arab forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated a Byzantine expedition at Ajnadayn in 634, and after a siege of six months they took Damascus, which Heraclius later retook. The Arabs won the Battle of Yarmuk in 636, and Heraclius reportedly gave up Syria. The general Amr ibn al-As began the conquest of Egypt on his own initiative in 639 and won a major victory at Heliopolis in 640.

In the east, the Shah Yazdegerd III raised an army, though many marzbans refused to help, and it suffered a devastating defeat at the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah in 636. The Persian campaigns continued until 651. The assassination of Caliph Uthman in 656 began the first Muslim civil war, and conquests stopped for a time. After Ali was killed by the Kharijites in January 661, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan became caliph and founded the Umayyad dynasty, with its capital at Damascus.

The conquests broke the order dominated by the Sasanians in the east and the Byzantines in the west. Muslim armies overran the Sasanians and confined the Byzantines to part of Anatolia and Southeastern Europe. Over the following century Muslim rule reached across most of the Middle East and North Africa, parts of South Asia and Central Asia, and parts of Southern Europe. The historian James Buchan wrote that in speed and extent only Alexander the Great's conquests matched them, and that they lasted longer.

Explanations of the success are hard to establish, since only fragmentary sources survive. Fred Donner points to the first Islamic state, with its ideological coherence and mobilisation. Most historians add that the Sasanians and Byzantines were militarily exhausted. The new rulers generally followed the Middle Eastern pattern of religious pluralism, which was dominance by one group, not equality.
east-africa: East Africa is defined in varying ways. The United Nations Statistics Division counts 18 sovereign states and four territories. In a narrow sense it means Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda, which shared British administration; wider definitions add the Horn of Africa, made up of Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia and Somalia, the African Great Lakes, and island states such as the Comoros, Mauritius and the Seychelles.

The East African Rift shapes the landscape. The region holds Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya, the two tallest peaks in Africa, as well as Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika. The climate is mostly arid or semi-arid, with coastal regions leading up to cooler highlands where large population centres often lie.

The region is thought to be the foundation of humanity, with some of the earliest evidence of human ancestors in highland areas such as the Rift Valley. Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Somalia and the Red Sea coast of Sudan are considered the most likely location of Punt, which had close relations with Egypt in the times of Pharaoh Sahure and Queen Hatshepsut. The Kingdom of Aksum, a trading empire centred on Eritrea and northern Ethiopia, existed from approximately 100 to 940 CE, minted its own currency and established hegemony over the declining Kingdom of Kush.

The Bantu expansion, a mass migration between 2500 and 3000 years ago, shaped the population. Sea routes to the Arab regions and India led to cultural mixing on the Swahili coast, where the Swahili language developed with loan words from Arabic. Vasco da Gama visited Mombasa in 1498, and the Portuguese presence officially began after 1505, when Don Francisco de Almeida conquered Kilwa; English and German colonies followed.

In the Horn of Africa Afroasiatic languages predominate, among them Oromo, Somali, Amharic and Tigrinya. In the Great Lakes region Bantu languages are most widely spoken, and Swahili is a trade language with official status in Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda. Christianity and Islam are the predominant religions, alongside traditional African religions.
east-african-community: Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda have cooperated since the early 20th century. The East African Currency Board provided a common currency from 1919 to 1966. A customs union between Kenya and Uganda in 1917, which Tanganyika joined in 1927, was followed by the East African High Commission from 1948 to 1961, the East African Common Services Organization from 1961 to 1967, and the East African Community from 1967 to 1977. The organisation was founded in 1967, collapsed in 1977 and was revived on 7 July 2000.

Burundi and Rwanda joined the community in 2009, the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2022 and Somalia in 2024, and South Sudan was invited to apply at its independence in 2011. Its main objective is regional economic integration. In 2008, after negotiations with two other regional bodies, it agreed to an expanded free trade area, and in 2010 it launched a common market for goods, labour and capital. A protocol signed in 2013 outlined plans for a monetary union, and the community is regarded as a potential precursor to an East African Federation with its capital at Arusha, Tanzania.

The Treaty for the Establishment of the East African Community created seven organs. The Summit, made up of the heads of state, gives strategic direction, decides by consensus and admits new members. The Council of ministers implements its decisions. The East African Court of Justice is the judicial arm, and the East African Legislative Assembly, inaugurated in 2001 with 27 members elected by the national parliaments, is the legislative arm. The Secretariat is the executive organ, headed by a Secretary General appointed for a single five-year term. The customs union rests on a common external tariff, duty-free trade between members and common customs procedures.
east-asia: East Asia is a geocultural region of Asia. It borders North Asia to the north, Southeast Asia to the south, South Asia to the south-west and Central Asia to the west, with the Pacific Ocean to the east. In common usage it covers Greater China, Japan, Korea and Mongolia. China, Japan and Korea are its three core countries and civilisations, since they once shared a written language, a culture and a Confucian system of values instituted by imperial China. Some scholars include Vietnam, part of the wider Chinese cultural sphere, though many organisations class it as Southeast Asian.

Chinese civilisation is regarded as one of the earliest cradles of civilisation, and for thousands of years China was the leading civilisation of the region. Han China's northeastern expansion in 108 BCE took the northern part of the Korean peninsula, and Chinese writing, coinage, rice culture and Confucian political institutions took root in Korea. Japan adopted Chinese characters from the fourth century. Chinese influence was strongest under the Tang dynasty, and in 645 Prince Naka no Ōe launched the Taika Reform, remaking the Japanese bureaucracy on the Tang model. From the 3rd to the 18th century a tributary system governed relations: the Chinese emperor received tribute and in return conferred legitimacy on other rulers and gave gifts such as porcelain and silk.

China's power declined as contacts with the West grew in the late 19th century. Commodore Matthew C. Perry opened Japan to Western influence, and after the Meiji Restoration Japan became the first industrialised nation in East Asia. It defeated the Qing dynasty in the First Sino-Japanese War and Russia in 1905. During World War II, Japan brought Korea, Taiwan, much of eastern China, Manchuria, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia under its control. The People's Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October 1949, and the Republic of China government withdrew to Taiwan. The Korean peninsula was partitioned, and the Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953.

The major languages are Mandarin Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and the major religions include Mahayana Buddhism, Confucianism, Taoism and Chinese folk religion, with Shinto in Japan. The region has around 1.65 billion inhabitants. The Chinese calendar is the root of many other East Asian calendars, and East Asian vocabularies and scripts are often derived from Classical Chinese.
east-francia: In August 843, after three years of civil war following the death of Emperor Louis the Pious, the Treaty of Verdun was signed by his three sons. The division was largely based on the Meuse, Scheldt, Saone and Rhone rivers. Lothair I kept the imperial title and Middle Francia, Charles the Bald received West Francia, and Louis the German received the eastern, mostly Germanic-speaking lands: the Duchy of Saxony, Austrasia, Alamannia, the Duchy of Bavaria and the March of Carinthia. Regino of Prüm wrote that its different peoples could be told apart by race, customs, language and laws.

In 869 Lotharingia was divided between West and East Francia by the Treaty of Meerssen. In 888 nobles deposed Charles the Fat, who had briefly reunited the Frankish lands, and Arnulf of Carinthia was elected king in the East. As royal power weakened, the dukes of Bavaria, Swabia, Franconia, Saxony and Lotharingia became hereditary rulers of their territories.

On 10 November 911 Saxon, Franconian, Bavarian and Swabian nobles, no longer electing a Carolingian, chose one of their own, Conrad I. He struggled to establish authority over the other dukes, and on his deathbed named Henry of Saxony as his successor. Henry subdued the dukes and built a state apparatus that his son Otto I used fully. After Otto was crowned emperor in Rome in 962, the era of the Holy Roman Empire began.

Because Louis the German received none of the Carolingian regalia, the symbols and rituals of East Frankish kingship were created anew. The kingdom had a more formal notion of royal election than West Francia, and a coronation liturgy of about 900 has the people asked whether they will obey the king and answer Fiat, fiat. By the 12th century Otto of Freising had to explain that the eastern kingdom of the Franks was now called the kingdom of the Germans. The division, reinforced by the language split between Germanic and Latin speech, gradually hardened into separate kingdoms: East Francia became the Kingdom of Germany and West Francia the Kingdom of France.
east-germany: At the Yalta Conference the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union agreed to divide defeated Germany into occupation zones. The Soviet zone comprised the five states of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia. Cooperation among the four powers broke down quickly, and the Soviets withdrew from the Allied Control Council in 1948. On 21 April 1946 the Communist and Social Democratic parties in the Soviet zone merged to form the Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED), under strong Soviet pressure on the Social Democrats. The SED won the elections of October 1946 and nationalised infrastructure and industrial plants. The state itself was formed on 7 October 1949.

Emigration to the West was a serious problem, since many emigrants were well-educated young people; about a quarter of East Germans left before the Berlin Wall was completed in 1961. The government fortified the inner German border and built the Wall, and many people attempting to flee were killed by border guards or booby traps such as landmines. In 1961 to 1970 the state was stable, and the Honecker era of 1971 to 1985 saw closer ties with West Germany.

In May 1989, after anger over faked local election results, many citizens left the country, helped by the removal of the fence on Hungary's border with Austria on 2 May. Peaceful protests beginning in Leipzig led to the fall of the Berlin Wall, and a free election was held in 1990. The five states joined the Federal Republic under Article 23 of the Basic Law, and East Berlin united with West Berlin on 3 October 1990.

The state described itself as a socialist workers' and peasants' state, ruled by the SED. Its economy was centrally planned, it joined the Comecon trade bloc in 1950, and despite heavy reparations to the Soviet Union it became the most successful economy of the Eastern Bloc. A State Secretariat for Church Affairs handled contact with churches from 1957. All artistic and literary expression was subject to state censorship. Historians describe the regime as authoritarian, and several leaders, among them Egon Krenz, were later prosecuted for offences committed in the GDR era.
east-india-company: The company grew out of English interest in the Indian Ocean trade after Francis Drake's voyage of 1577-1580, which reached the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, and returned a profit to investors of some 5,000 per cent. In September 1599 a group of merchants and sea-farers, including Thomas Smythe, resolved to invest £30,133 in a voyage to the East Indies, and later raised their investment to £68,373. The company was chartered as the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies, with Smythe as its first governor.

Sir James Lancaster commanded the first voyage in 1601. In the Malacca Straits he took a rich Portuguese carrack, the Sao Thome, and the proceeds allowed the voyagers to set up trading posts, called factories, at Bantam on Java and in the Moluccas. Lancaster was knighted by James I on his return in 1603.

In 1694 an act allowed any English firm to trade with India, annulling a charter that had stood for almost 100 years. A second company was floated in 1697 with a state-backed indemnity of £2 million, but the stockholders of the old company subscribed heavily in it and dominated it.

In the Seven Years' War (1756-1763) Robert Clive led the company to victory over the French commander Joseph François Dupleix. After the Battle of Plassey in 1757 the areas ruled by the company gradually expanded, and by 1858 most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, with Lower Burma, was ruled by the company or by princely states tied to it by treaty. At its peak its three presidency armies totalled about 260,000 soldiers.
Company rule had severe costs. The company used torture to extract taxes, and it mishandled the Great Bengal famine of 1770, in which an estimated 10 million people starved to death.

In 1833 the company gave up its commercial trading assets in India to the British government, which took on its debts. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the Government of India Act 1858 had the Crown take over its Indian possessions, administration and armies. It lingered in vestigial form, managing the tea trade for the government, until it was dissolved on 1 June 1874. The Times wrote in 1873 that it had accomplished a work such as no other trading company ever attempted.
east-indies: European exploration of the region began in the last three years of the 15th century and continued into the 16th, led by Portuguese explorers after the Cape Route had been found. The Portuguese called the whole region they reached the Indies. Christopher Columbus, who had grossly underestimated the westward distance from Europe to Asia, at first took the New World for the easternmost part of the Indies. To avoid confusion the Americas came to be called the West Indies, also the New Indies or Little Indies, and the original Indies the East Indies, also the Old Indies or Great Indies.

The term has had a broad and a narrow sense. In the Age of Discovery it covered the coasts of the Indian subcontinent and the Indochinese Peninsula together with the Malay Archipelago. In the narrow sense it meant the Malay Archipelago alone, which today comprises the Indonesian Archipelago, New Guinea and the Philippine Archipelago. The former Dutch New Guinea, however, is geographically counted as part of Melanesia and is not included.

Parts of the region are sometimes named after the colonial empire that held them. The Spanish East Indies, the Philippines, were Spanish territory for 333 years before the American conquest and later independence. The Dutch East Indies kept that name for about 300 years until Indonesian independence, and British East Indies refers to Malaysia. The term may also take in the former French Indochina, the former British territories of Brunei, Hong Kong and Singapore, and the former Portuguese Macau and Timor.

The peoples of the region are culturally very diverse and do not consider themselves a single ethnic group. Most are Austronesians, whose ancestors first expanded from the island of Taiwan. In the early modern period Han Chinese began to migrate south and became known as the Peranakans or Straits Chinese. Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism are the most widespread religions.

After the founding of European trading companies in the 17th century, among them the British East India Company and the Dutch East India Company, the Indies were important sources of trade goods, particularly cotton, indigo and spices. The name East Indian was once applied to people of all the East Indies, to keep them apart from the indigenous peoples of the Americas, who were then simply called Indians. In colonial times South-East Asians who were not from India were also called Indians. Today the inhabitants of the region are not called East Indians.
east-java: East Java is a province of Indonesia in the easternmost third of the island of Java. Its only land border is with Central Java in the west. The Java Sea and the Indian Ocean lie along its northern and southern coasts, and the narrow Bali Strait to the east separates Java from Bali. The province also includes the island of Madura, the Kangean islands and the Masalembu archipelago. Its two main rivers are the Brantas, 290 kilometres long, and the Solo, 548 kilometres long.

East Java has been inhabited since prehistoric times, as fossils found at Mojokerto, Trinil and Wajak show. The Dinoyo inscriptions found near Malang, dating from 760 CE, are the oldest written sources in East Java and tell of events in the Kingdom of Kanjuruhan. In 1222 Ken Arok founded the Kingdom of Singhasari, which he ruled until 1227. His descendants became kings of Singhasari and Majapahit from the 13th until the 15th century.

The date when Islam entered Java is unclear. Some experts place it around the 11th century, on the evidence of the tomb of Fatimah Binti Maimun at Leran, dated to 1085 CE, which also shows that Arab traders frequented the north coast. Islam gradually supplanted Hinduism in the 14th and 15th centuries, and the last nobles and people of the fallen Majapahit fled to Bali. A Dutch expedition of four ships under Cornelis de Houtman in 1596 began the Dutch presence on the island, and by the end of the 18th century the Dutch had expanded their influence over the Islamic sultanates in the interior of Java.

The capital is Surabaya, the second largest city in Indonesia and a major industrial and business centre. East Java is Indonesia's second most populous province after West Java. Most of the population is Muslim, with Hindu communities among the Tenggerese and the Balinese. Indonesian is the official language, but Javanese and Madurese are most frequently used. The Suramadu Bridge connects Surabaya with Madura.
east-kalimantan: East Kalimantan covers the eastern part of Borneo. Its Cape Mangkalihat separates the Makassar Strait from the Celebes Sea, and it borders South, Central and West Kalimantan and, by a short land border, Sarawak in Malaysia. Its northernmost region was split off on 25 October 2012 and inaugurated on 15 April 2013 as the separate province of North Kalimantan. The province has hundreds of rivers, which carry much of its transport, and the longest is the Mahakam. Samarinda, its capital, is the most populous city on the island of Borneo. It was once mostly covered by tropical rainforest, but illegal logging has removed much of it.

A limestone cave called Lubang Jeriji Saléh holds paintings that a team led by Maxime Aubert and Pindi Setiawan reported in Nature in 2018 to be the oldest known figurative art in the world. The French explorer Luc-Henri Fage and the archaeologist Jean-Michel Chazine first noticed them in 1994.

The Kingdom of Kutai Martadipura, founded in the 4th century CE, is the first and oldest Hindu kingdom of Indonesia, and the Sultanate of Kutai ing Martadipura succeeded it in the 14th century. The Sultanate of Pasir was another kingdom in the region. Between 1620 and 1624 kingdoms in East Kalimantan came under the influence of Sultan Alauddin of Makassar, and people from South Sulawesi began to arrive. On 1 January 1817 Sultan Sulaiman of Banjar handed East Kalimantan over to the Dutch East Indies, and in 1846 the Dutch placed a Resident Assistant at Samarinda. The province was established by Law No. 25 of 1956 from the special regions of Berau, Bulongan and Kutai.

Oil, natural gas, coal and gold underpin the economy; the Mahakam River delta holds fields such as Attaka, Badak and Handil, and Balikpapan has an oil refinery built before the Second World War, destroyed in the war and rebuilt after Indonesian independence. Indonesian is used officially, and Banjarese serves as the common language between groups. Kutai Malay, Paser and Kenyah are among the other languages and are considered threatened. Migrants from Java, Sulawesi and South Kalimantan form a large part of the population. The site of the new national capital, Nusantara, lies within the province.
east-karelia: East Karelia, also called Eastern or Russian Karelia, is the part of Karelia beyond the eastern border of Finland which, since the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, has remained Eastern Orthodox and a part of Russia. It is distinguished from the western part, Finnish Karelia, which before 1808 was Swedish Karelia. It consists mainly of two old historical regions, Viena or White Karelia and Aunus or Olonets Karelia.

The Fennomans, ethnic nationalists of the 19th century, saw East Karelia as the ancient home of Finnic culture, untouched by Scandinavians or Slavs. In its sparsely populated backwoods, mainly in White Karelia, Elias Lönnrot (1802–1884) collected the folk tales that became the Kalevala, published from 1835 to 1849. The idea of joining the region to a Greater Finland had wide support in newly independent Finland after 1917.

When Finland and Soviet Russia divided Karelia between them in 1920, the Soviet authorities promised far-reaching cultural rights to the Finnic peoples who made up most of East Karelia's population. Within the Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic these rights were never realised, and under Stalin ethnic Finns were persecuted and an intensive programme of Russification began.

Annexation was most popular during the Continuation War of 1941–1944, when an expected German conquest of the Soviet Union made it seem feasible. Finnish forces occupied most of East Karelia from 1941 to 1944, and the war brought hardship to the local ethnic Russian civilians, including forced labour and internment in prison camps as enemy aliens. After the Moscow Armistice of September 1944 calls for annexation virtually disappeared.

Most of East Karelia is now part of the Republic of Karelia within the Russian Federation. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, Finnic culture in the region has experienced a revival. In Finnish the region is called Itä-Karjala or Venäjän Karjala, and in Karelian Idä-Karjala.
east-lothian: East Lothian lies south of the Firth of Forth in the eastern central Lowlands of Scotland, bordering Edinburgh to the west and the Scottish Borders to the south. It is predominantly rural, with 40 miles of coastline along which lie Musselburgh, Prestonpans, North Berwick and Dunbar. Off the coast north of North Berwick are small islands, the largest being Fidra, Lamb, Craigleith and Bass Rock. To the south the Lammermuir Hills mark the boundary with Berwickshire. Its county town is Haddington and its largest town is Musselburgh.

After the end of Roman occupation, Lothian was populated by Brythonic-speaking Britons and formed part of the kingdom of the Gododdin. In the 7th century the Angles took it, and it became part of Bernicia, then of Northumbria. It came under the Scottish monarchy in the 10th century. Haddington, Dunbar and North Berwick became royal burghs, and Alexander II was born at the Palace of Haddington in 1198.

The county lay on the route of repeated wars between England and Scotland. Edward I's forces won the Battle of Dunbar in 1296, and in 1650 Oliver Cromwell's Parliamentary forces defeated Covenanter forces at another Battle of Dunbar. In September 1745 the Jacobites under Charles Edward Stuart won a significant victory over Sir John Cope at the Battle of Prestonpans, before their defeat at Culloden in April 1746.

The county was called Haddingtonshire until 1921, when its name was changed to East Lothian. It became a district of Lothian Region in 1975 and one of Scotland's 32 council areas in 1996. Its economy has long been agricultural, with fishing and coal-mining also significant, and Dunbar, Tantallon and Dirleton castles date from its medieval and early modern conflicts.
east-pakistan: East Pakistan was the eastern province of Pakistan, restructured and renamed from the province of East Bengal, and it covered the territory of present-day Bangladesh. Its land borders were with India and Burma, with a coastline on the Bay of Bengal. In contrast to the desert and mountains of West Pakistan, it had the world's largest delta, about 700 rivers and tropical hilly jungles, and its heavy rainfall made rice, tea and jute the main crops. It held 55 per cent of Pakistan's population, and Bengalis were its largest ethnic group.

The One Unit scheme of Prime Minister Mohammad Ali Bogra merged the four western provinces into West Pakistan, and East Bengal became East Pakistan. The Constitution of 1956 made Pakistan an Islamic republic. In 1958 General Ayub Khan seized power in a military coup and ruled for eleven years. In 1966 Sheikh Mujibur Rahman of the Awami League announced the six-point movement in Lahore, demanding greater autonomy and the restoration of democracy; he was indicted for treason in the Agartala Conspiracy Case and released during the uprising of 1969, which contributed to Ayub Khan's resignation.

Ayub Khan's government built the Kaptai Dam in 1965 and the Eastern Refinery at Chittagong, and Dacca was named a second capital, with the American architect Louis Kahn hired to design the national assembly complex. Yet, according to the World Bank, the province suffered economic discrimination, with higher government spending on West Pakistan and the East's foreign exchange surpluses used to pay for the West's imports, although the East generated a major share of exports.

General Yahya Khan replaced Ayub Khan and organised the general election of 1970. The Bhola cyclone of that year claimed about half a million lives, and resentment of the federal government grew. The Awami League won the largest number of seats, but the military junta stalled in accepting the result. Civil disobedience followed, then the Bangladesh Liberation War, the genocide of Bengalis and the persecution of Biharis.
In Pakistan the secession came as a severe shock and a humiliating defeat for the armed forces. East Pakistan's territory became the independent state of Bangladesh, a name meaning country of Bengal.
east-prussia: The landscape of East Prussia was gently rolling plains and small hills, flatter in the north and with more hills in the south, notably in Masuria. In the north-west the province bordered the Baltic Sea, from which the Vistula Spit and the Curonian Spit separated the Vistula Lagoon and the Curonian Lagoon. Most of the province's rivers, among them the Pregel and the Memel, emptied into the lagoons. Its people included Germans, Masurians, Poles in the south and Lithuanian-speaking Prussians in the north-east.

In the 13th century the Teutonic Knights took possession of Prussia and created a monastic state to administer the conquered Old Prussians. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach converted to Lutheranism, secularised the Prussian branch of the Order and became the first duke of the Duchy of Prussia, a vassal of the Polish crown. The duchy passed to the Electors of Brandenburg in 1618, and in 1701 Elector Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia.

After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the former Ducal Prussia, enlarged by Warmia, was designated East Prussia by decree of 31 January 1773. By the Treaty of Tilsit of 9 July 1807 Prussia lost almost half its territory. Between 1829 and 1878 the province was joined with West Prussia. In the First World War the Russian Army invaded in 1914 and was defeated at Tannenberg in 1914 and the Second Battle of the Masurian Lakes in 1915. The Treaty of Versailles made the province an exclave, and Lithuania annexed the Memel Territory in 1923.

After Nazi Germany's defeat in 1945 East Prussia was divided between the Soviet Union and Poland under the Potsdam Conference. The northern part became the Kaliningrad Oblast of the Russian republic in 1946, when Königsberg was renamed Kaliningrad, and the Klaipėda Region went to the Lithuanian republic. Most of the German population left in the evacuation at the end of the war, and an estimated 300,000 died in the bombing, the fighting and through mistreatment, hunger, cold and disease. The remainder were expelled in accordance with the Potsdam Agreement.
east-slavs: Little is known of the East Slavs before about 859 CE, when the first events recorded in the Primary Chronicle occurred. They apparently lacked a written language, and the few known facts come from archaeology, foreign travellers' accounts and the comparison of Slavic languages. Scholars have no consensus on the original homeland of the Slavs. By 600 CE the Slavs had split linguistically into southern, western and eastern branches, and by the 8th century they were the dominant ethnic group on the East European Plain. The Primary Chronicle lists twelve tribal unions settled by the 10th century between the Western Bug, the Dnieper and the Black Sea, among them the Polans, Drevlyans, Krivichs and Severians.

The East Slavs practised slash-and-burn agriculture, clearing forest with fire and moving on after a few years, which explains their rapid spread. One stream settled along the Dnieper and spread north to the northern Volga valley. Another moved north-east, met the Varangians of the Rus' Khaganate and established Novgorod, which the chronicle dates to 862. They formed the majority of the population of Kievan Rus'.

Its fragmentation in the 11th century caused population shifts that hastened the differentiation of the Rus' people into Ukrainians, Belarusians and Russians. In the south-west and west, under Lithuanian and later Polish influence, Ruthenian, Ukrainian and Belarusian identities developed, while Russian identity developed in the Muscovite north-east and the Novgorodian north.

The East Slavs speak East Slavic languages and live chiefly in Eastern Europe, extending across northern Asia to the Pacific. The existing groups are the Belarusians, Russians and Ukrainians. Rusyns are sometimes considered a separate nation, though often a subgroup of Ukrainians, and Don Cossacks likewise a subgroup of Russians. They consider Kievan Rus' their cultural ancestor.
east-west-schism: The split between Western and Eastern Christians came from political, cultural and theological factors over centuries, and historians regard the mutual excommunications of 1054 as its terminal event. In 330 Emperor Constantine moved the imperial capital to Byzantium, later Constantinople, and Rome lost its status as the imperial capital. The First Council of Constantinople in 381 raised the see of Constantinople above Alexandria and Antioch, which has been described as sowing the seed of the later rivalry.

In 732 Emperor Leo III the Isaurian, angered by Pope Gregory III's opposition to his iconoclast policy, transferred Sicily, Calabria and Illyria from the patriarchate of Rome to that of Constantinople. The West's rejection of the Quinisext Council of 692 led to pressure on it to give up Latin customs such as fasting on Saturdays and using unleavened bread.

In 1053 Leo of Ohrid wrote a letter meant for all the Latin bishops, including the pope, attacking Western practices such as unleavened bread in the Eucharist. According to J. B. Bury he did so at the instigation of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius, who himself closed all the Latin churches in Constantinople. In 1054 a legate sent by Pope Leo IX travelled to the city to deny Cerularius the title of ecumenical patriarch and to insist that he recognise the pope as head of all the churches. The legation also sought help from Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos against the Normans, who had conquered southern Italy.

When the legation's leader, Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, learned that Cerularius refused, he excommunicated him, and Cerularius excommunicated Humbert and the other legates. The legates' act is of doubtful validity, since Pope Leo had died.

There was no single event that marked the breakdown; the two churches slid into and out of schism over several centuries, with temporary reconciliations. It is estimated that in 1054 a slim majority of Christians worldwide were Eastern, and Timothy Ware observes that ordinary Christians in both East and West were largely unaware of the dispute. Scholars have proposed other dates for the schism, including 1009, 1204, 1277 and 1484.

At the Second Council of Lyon in 1272 Michael VIII pledged to reunite the churches. At the Council of Ferrara-Florence, on 6 June 1439, all the Eastern bishops present but one, Mark of Ephesus, signed an agreement accepting Western doctrines, but it bore no lasting fruit. The Eastern Catholic Churches consider themselves to have reconciled East and West by accepting the primacy of the Bishop of Rome while keeping Eastern liturgical practice.
easter-island: Easter Island is a volcanic island at the south-eastern point of the Polynesian Triangle. It consists mainly of three extinct coalesced volcanoes: Terevaka, 507 metres high, forms the bulk of the island, while Poike and Rano Kau form the eastern and southern headlands and give it a roughly triangular shape. It is one of the most isolated inhabited islands in the world. The nearest inhabited land is Pitcairn Island, with about 50 residents, and the nearest continental point is in central Chile, 3,512 kilometres away. The island was once forested, with a large extinct palm among its dominant trees.

Oral tradition says the island was first settled by a two-canoe expedition under the chief Hotu Matu'a and his captain Tu'u ko Iho, who left a homeland after Hotu lost three battles to a neighbouring chief. Estimates of the date of settlement have ranged from 400 to 1300 CE, and radiocarbon work puts it late, about 1200 CE. Land clearing for cultivation and the Polynesian rat, which the settlers brought, contributed to deforestation, and large areas show palm stumps cut by people. The settlers made the moai from local stone, using red scoria from Puna Pau for the topknots called pukao and obsidian for the eyes.

The population was estimated at 2,000 to 3,000 when the Dutch navigator Jacob Roggeveen arrived on Easter Sunday, 5 April 1722, giving the island its European name. His visit killed about a dozen islanders. Spanish ships came in 1770, and James Cook in 1774 reported that some statues had been toppled; he learned that the statues commemorated former high chiefs.

In December 1862 Peruvian slave raiders captured around 1,500 men and women, half of the island's population, among them the paramount chief, his heir and those who could read the rongorongo script. When the survivors were repatriated, smallpox spread from Easter Island to the Marquesas. The population fell to a low of 111 native inhabitants in 1877. Chile annexed the island in 1888. In 1914 an uprising, inspired by the catechist María Angata Veri Veri and led by Daniel Maria Teave, sought state action against the company running the island.

Easter Island is a special territory of Chile, a status given in 2007, and part of the Valparaíso Region. The Rapa Nui were granted Chilean citizenship in 1966. The 2017 census registered 7,750 people, 45 per cent of whom identified as Rapa Nui. Spanish is an official language, the only such case in Polynesia. UNESCO named the island a World Heritage Site in 1995, and much of it lies within Rapa Nui National Park, which protects nearly 1,000 moai.
easter-rising: The Acts of Union 1800 had joined the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland, abolishing the Irish Parliament. Many Irish nationalists opposed the union, and further rebellions followed the Irish Rebellion of 1798, in 1803, 1848 and 1867; all failed. The Supreme Council of the Irish Republican Brotherhood met on 5 September 1914, just over a month after Britain declared war on Germany, and resolved to stage an uprising before the war ended and to seek help from Germany.

In May 1915 Tom Clarke and Seán Mac Diarmada set up a Military Council, which worked independently of those who thought a rising inopportune. The Volunteer chief of staff, Eoin MacNeill, would support one only if the British tried to suppress the Volunteers or introduce conscription.

Pearse ordered three days of 'parades and manoeuvres' from Easter Sunday as a cover for the rising. A German ship carrying 20,000 rifles, disguised as the Norwegian Aud, was sent to County Kerry, but the arms did not arrive, and MacNeill issued a countermand that cut the number who mobilised. On Monday 24 April about 1,200 Irish Volunteers and Irish Citizen Army members, with women of Cumann na mBan, took buildings in central Dublin and proclaimed the Irish Republic. The British brought in thousands of reinforcements, artillery and a gunboat. Fighting on the routes into the centre slowed the British advance, and the rebel positions were gradually surrounded and shelled.

Shelling set fire to the General Post Office, and the garrison, under Pearse because James Connolly had been wounded, withdrew to 16 Moore Street. Pearse agreed to an unconditional surrender on Saturday 29 April. Outside Dublin there were isolated actions, such as the Fingal Battalion's attacks on police barracks near Ashbourne and the brief hold on Enniscorthy by Volunteers. At least 485 people died, according to the Glasnevin Trust: 260 civilians, 143 British military and police personnel, and 82 rebels. Many civilians were killed by British artillery fire or mistaken for rebels.

The country stayed under martial law. 3,430 men and 79 women were arrested, and sixteen leaders were executed from May 1916 after courts martial. On 25 April the pacifist Francis Sheehy Skeffington was arrested and next day shot on the orders of Captain John Bowen-Colthurst, who was found guilty but insane. At first many Dubliners were hostile to the rebels, who were blamed for the destruction. Opposition to the British reaction later changed opinion. Sinn Féin won 73 of the 105 Irish seats in the general election of 14 December 1918, and its members met on 21 January 1919 as Dáil Éireann and adopted a Declaration of Independence.
eastern-cape: The Eastern Cape is the second-largest province of South Africa, with an area of 168,966 square kilometres. It grows progressively wetter from west to east. The west is mostly semi-arid Karoo, apart from temperate rainforest in the far south around Tsitsikamma. Most of the province between Graaff-Reinet and Rhodes is hilly to very mountainous, with the Sneeuberge, Stormberge, Winterberge and Drakensberg. The highest point is Ben Macdhui at 3,001 metres. The east, from East London and Queenstown towards the KwaZulu-Natal border, was previously known as Transkei and is lush grassland on rolling hills cut by deep gorges.

The central and eastern part of the province is the traditional home of the Xhosa people. The Xhosa Kingdom was one of the most powerful kingdoms in Africa and had all the states of the Eastern Cape as tributaries. Any group that recognised the Xhosa Kingdom as paramount became Xhosa, practised Xhosa culture and used isiXhosa as its main language. The peoples counted as Xhosa include the AmaMpondo, AbaThembu, AmaMpondomise, AmaHlubi, AmaBhaca, AmaXesibe and AmaBomvana.

In the late 18th century the Dutch Cape Colony expanded slowly eastwards from Cape Town, and in 1786 the Dutch settlement of Graaff-Reinet was established, named after the governor Cornelius Jacob van de Graaff and his wife Hester Cornelia, née Reynet. During the Napoleonic Wars Britain took control of the Cape Colony in 1806 and encouraged British citizens to migrate there to increase the British population. In 1820 the area, then known as the Xhosa Kingdom, began to be settled by Europeans from Great Britain and Ireland.

From the early 1800s until the Union of South Africa was formed in 1910, British migrants colonised the Eastern Cape. They founded most of its towns, naming them after places in the United Kingdom, members of the royal family or their own founders, and built schools, churches, hospitals and government buildings. Among the older settlements are Grahamstown (1812), Cradock (1814), Fort Beaufort (1814), Port Elizabeth, Salem and Bathurst (all 1820), East London (1836) and King William's Town (1836).

The province was formed in 1994 from the Xhosa homelands, or bantustans, of Transkei and Ciskei together with the eastern portion of the Cape Province. Its capital is Bhisho and its largest city is Gqeberha, formerly Port Elizabeth. The 2022 census counted 7,230,204 people, with Xhosa the first language of 81.8%. The province was home to many anti-apartheid leaders, among them Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Steve Biko and Robert Sobukwe. Its attractions include 800 kilometres of coastline, Addo Elephant National Park, created in 1931, and the National Arts Festival in Makhanda, formerly Grahamstown.
eastern-europe: Eastern Europe is a subregion of the European continent, and the term is largely ambiguous. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, while its western boundary is defined in many ways and has shifted over time. Much of the region lies on the East European Plain, whose highest point, in the Valdai Hills northwest of Moscow, reaches only 343 metres. It is drained by long rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, the Dnieper and the Danube. The historian Larry Wolff has argued that the idea of Eastern Europe was created in the 18th century by Enlightenment thinkers.

The region's history was shaped by the migrations of the Slavs in the 6th and 7th centuries and by the Christianization of its peoples from both Rome and Constantinople. A treaty of 681 recognizing the rule of the Bulgars marks the beginning of the Bulgarian state. In 882 Oleg made Kyiv the capital of Kievan Rus', the first East Slavic state, and in 964–965 Sviatoslav destroyed the Khazar capitals. The Mongol invasions, and later the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, shaped its political map.

In 1526 Suleiman destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, and the Ottoman advance in Central Europe ended at the siege of Vienna in 1683. In June 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia with about 600,000 troops, of whom fewer than 30,000 returned. After the First World War new or restored states emerged, among them Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact of 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union divided the region into spheres of influence.

From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and during the Cold War the term Eastern Europe was used almost as a synonym for the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc; historians generally regard definitions based on that usage as outdated. After the Revolutions of 1989 many countries joined NATO and the European Union: the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia entered the Union on 1 May 2004, Bulgaria and Romania on 1 January 2007, and Croatia on 1 July 2013. The region's traditions include Orthodox icon painting, the literature of Alexander Pushkin and Adam Mickiewicz, and the music of Frédéric Chopin.
eastern-thrace: Eastern Thrace is the eastern part of the historical region of Thrace and the part of Turkey that lies in south-east Europe, with an area of 23,764 km2, about 3% of the country's land. The Dardanelles, the Sea of Marmara and the Bosphorus separate it from Anatolia. It includes the provinces of Edirne, Tekirdağ and Kırklareli and the European parts of Çanakkale and Istanbul. Its southernmost part is the Gallipoli peninsula. Greece lies to the west and Bulgaria to the north, with the Aegean Sea to the south-west and the Black Sea to the north-east. Its position beside a major sea trade corridor has long given it importance.

Myth placed Hero and Leander at the ancient city of Sestus and made Aeneas the founder of Aenus. After the death of Alexander the Great, his general Lysimachus (360 to 281 BCE) became king of Thrace and made Lysimachia his capital. The Battle of Adrianople in 378 was a turning point in the decline of the Roman Empire. Çimpe Castle, taken in 1352, was the first European territory held by the Ottoman Empire, and Edirne became its second capital after Bursa. The Gallipoli Campaign of the First World War was fought on the peninsula.

Ottoman Rumelia was lost piecemeal from 1699, and the bulk of it in the First Balkan War of 1912. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878 and the Balkan Wars, Muslim refugees (muhacir) of various origins were forced to flee from the Balkans towards Eastern Thrace through expulsions, violence and massacres, and further emigration followed the population exchange between Greece and Turkey that followed. The land borders were defined by the Treaty of Constantinople of 1913 and the Bulgarian-Ottoman convention of 1915, and were reaffirmed by the Treaty of Lausanne.

Its largest city is Istanbul. Edirne holds the Selimiye Mosque, the Üç Şerefeli Mosque, the Old Mosque, the Muradiye Mosque and the Grand Synagogue. The Kırkpınar oil-wrestling tournament has been held near Edirne every year since 1360, and the Romani festival Kakava is held annually in Edirne and Kırklareli. A large part of the population descends from the muhacir who settled there.
eastern-turkestan: East Turkestan is a loosely defined geographical region in what is now the north-west of the People's Republic of China, at the crossroads of East and Central Asia. The name was coined in the 19th century by Russian Turkologists, among them Nikita Bichurin, to replace the Western term 'Chinese Turkestan', which referred to the Tarim Basin in southern Xinjiang. From the 17th century the Uyghur name for the Tarim Basin was Altishahr, Six Cities. Chinese dynasties from the Han to the Tang called an overlapping area the Western Regions. Until the 20th century local people tended to name themselves after their cities or oases, such as Kashgaria out of Kashgar.

In 60 BCE the Han dynasty established the Protectorate of the Western Regions over the oasis states of the Tarim Basin, ruled indirectly through small agricultural military colonies. Chinese authority lapsed after the Western Han, was restored in 94 CE and lasted officially until 107 CE. The Western Turkic Khaganate inherited the region after the Gökturks, and western Tujue territory later became part of the Tang dynasty until the ninth century. In the sixteenth century the Chagatai Khanate completed the conversion to Islam and Turkification of western Xinjiang, then known as Moghulistan, while the Ming dynasty held the eastern areas.

In 1755 the Qing dynasty defeated the Dzungar Khanate and took two territories: Dzungaria in the north, where the Dzungars lived, and the southern areas, called Huijiang or Altishahr. In 1764 the Qianlong Emperor made Xinjiang an official name for the two together, and after General Tso suppressed the Dungan revolt, Xinjiang was reorganised as a province in 1882. Russia occupied the Ili valley between 1851 and 1881. After the Qing fell in 1912, Yang Zengxin took control and acceded to the Republic of China.

On 12 November 1933 Uyghur separatists in the Kashgar region declared the East Turkestan Republic, which lasted until 16 April 1934 and was recognised by no country; the warlord Sheng Shicai defeated it. A second East Turkestan Republic existed in the Ili region from 12 November 1944 to 27 June 1946, with Soviet support. In 1949 the Communist leadership persuaded both the Kuomintang and Republic governments in Xinjiang to surrender, and on 1 October 1955 Xinjiang was made the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
ebla: Ebla is a tell, now called Tell Mardikh, about 55 kilometres south-west of Aleppo. The name may derive from a Semitic word meaning white rock, possibly the limestone outcrop on which the city stood. In its first kingdom it covered 56 hectares behind mud-brick fortifications, with a raised acropolis in the centre and a lower town divided into four districts, each with its own gate. The city's patron god was Kura.

Ebla was first settled around 3500 BCE, and its growth was supported by satellite agricultural settlements and its role in growing international trade, which probably began with demand for wool in Sumer. Its first kingdom, between about 3000 and 2300 BCE, was the most prominent among the Syrian states. Its government consisted of a king, styled Malikum, and a grand vizier who headed a council of elders, and the queen shared the running of state affairs. The population in 2400 to 2300 BCE is estimated at about 40,000 in the capital. The palace was destroyed by fire during an Akkadian conquest.

A second kingdom continued the first under a new dynasty and was destroyed at the end of the 3rd millennium BCE. Amorites then formed a third kingdom, rebuilt as a planned city, whose first known king was Ibbit-Lim. It became a subject and ally of Yamhad until the Hittite king Mursili I destroyed Ebla around 1600 BCE.

Italian archaeologists directed by Paolo Matthiae began excavating Tell Mardikh in 1964. In 1968 they recovered a statue dedicated to the goddess Ishtar bearing the name of Ibbit-Lim, king of Ebla, which identified the city. The palace archive held about 20,000 cuneiform tablets dated to 2500 to 2350 BCE, in Sumerian and in Eblaite. They had been shelved by subject, and the positions of those that fell when the palace burned let the excavators reconstruct the shelving. Early claims of references to Yahweh and the Biblical Patriarchs are now widely discredited.
ebro-river: The Ebro rises at Fontibre in the Cantabrian Mountains of Cantabria, only 42 kilometres from the Bay of Biscay, and flows almost entirely east-south-east to the Mediterranean. It is the longest river entirely within Spain. Much of its water comes from northern tributaries that drain about two thirds of the southern slopes of the Pyrenees, and all of Andorra drains into it through the Segre. The valley is cut off from the sea by mountains, so the climate is dry and continental, with hot summers and cold winters.

The Greeks called the river Ibēr and the Romans Hibēr or Ibērus, and the Iberian Peninsula and its people took their names from it. After the First Punic War (264-241 BCE) it served as the dividing line between Roman expansion to the north and Carthaginian expansion to the south. When the Roman Republic, alarmed by Hannibal's growing influence, made the city of Saguntum, well south of the river, a protectorate of Rome, Hannibal saw a breach of that arrangement and used it as the occasion for the Second Punic War.

The Cistercian monastery of Nuestra Señora de Rueda, founded on the river's bank in Aragon in 1202, used one of the first large waterwheels built for power in Spain and diverted Ebro water to heat its buildings. In 1938 the river was the starting ground of the Battle of the Ebro, a Republican offensive of the Spanish Civil War that enjoyed early success but ended in defeat, the Republican forces never reaching their objective of Gandesa.

In Catalonia the river passes through gorges below the cliffs of the Serra de Cardó, turns east near Tortosa and reaches the sea close to Amposta. Dams were built at Flix in 1948 and at Mequinenza and Riba-roja in 1955. The delta in the Terres de l'Ebre region, about 340 square kilometres, is one of the largest wetlands of the western Mediterranean and has formed entirely from sediment carried downriver; Amposta, a seaport in the 4th century, now lies well inland. Part of it is protected as the Ebro Delta Natural Park, and it is farmed for rice, citrus fruit and vegetables.
ecomog: The members of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) agreed a Protocol on Mutual Defence Assistance at Freetown on 29 May 1981, which provided for an allied armed force when needed. ECOMOG itself was created by the Standing Mediation Committee at its meeting in Banjul on 6 and 7 August 1990. The Nigerian scholar Adekeye Adebajo has written that this body stood on shaky legal foundations, that the guidelines of the defence protocol were not followed, and that the force was justified largely on humanitarian grounds.

It was the English-speaking members of ECOWAS that acted, intervening in the Liberian civil war that had begun in 1989. Several French-speaking members strongly opposed the deployment, and the leaders of Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire supported Charles Taylor in his attempt to depose Samuel Doe.

Unlike the usual United Nations mission of the time, the force had to fight its way into a many-sided civil war to hold the factions apart. Most of its men and resources came from the Nigerian Armed Forces, with smaller units from Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone, The Gambia and others. Its first commander was the Ghanaian Lieutenant General Arnold Quainoo; after Samuel Doe was killed by Prince Johnson's Independent National Patriotic Front of Liberia on 9 September 1990, Major General Joshua Dogonyaro took over, the first of an unbroken line of Nigerian commanders.

Senegal sent 1,500 soldiers with some financial support from the United States, but withdrew them all by mid-January 1993, after six were killed in a confrontation with Taylor's supporters at Vahun on 28 May 1992. Corruption and organised looting by its troops led some Liberians to read the acronym as Every Car or Movable Object Gone. After Taylor was elected president on 19 July 1997, the last field commander, General Timothy Shelpidi, withdrew the force fully by the end of 1998.

Within Africa the force was the first credible attempt at a regional security initiative since the Organisation of African Unity tried to send an Inter-African Force to Chad in 1981. A deployment of 1,700 men planned in 2001 for the border between Guinea and Liberia never took place, for lack of funds and because of fighting in Liberia. In 2003, under pressure from the United States, ECOWAS launched a similar mission, ECOMIL, to halt the rebel occupation of Monrovia during the Second Liberian Civil War; it was soon succeeded by the United Nations mission UNMIL.
edfu: Edfu, called Behedet in ancient Egyptian and Apollonopolis Magna in Hellenistic and Roman times, lies on the west bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, between Esna and Aswan. The ancient settlement, Tell Edfu, lies about 50 m west of the Ptolemaic temple. The ruins of one of seven small provincial step pyramids built along the Nile Valley, loosely attributed to King Huni of the Third Dynasty, stand about 5 km to the south; the purpose of these pyramids is unknown.

Tell Edfu preserves a continuous sequence of occupation from the Old Kingdom to the Graeco-Roman period, more than 3,000 years, in places up to 20 m high, and holds evidence reaching back to the Predynastic Period. The settlement was the capital of the Second Upper Egypt nome. Its oldest datable part belongs to the late Old Kingdom, and it flourished and expanded westward during the First Intermediate Period, one of the few southern settlements to thrive while the north, especially the delta, seems to have been in economic decline.

Excavations have uncovered the administrative centre, a columned hall of the late Middle Kingdom, and a granary courtyard of the Second Intermediate Period with at least seven round silos, the largest found in an ancient Egyptian urban centre. A Sixth Dynasty governor, Izi, was worshipped as a god in the Middle Kingdom.

The god Horus was worshipped here as Horus Behedet. The Ptolemaic temple was built over the site of a smaller New Kingdom temple, which left the ruined pylon of the older building on the east side of the first court. Under the Roman emperors the city was the headquarters of the Legio II Traiana, and it later became a Christian bishopric, now a titular see of the Catholic Church.

The Temple of Horus is the most completely preserved of all temple remains in Egypt. In 1860 the French archaeologist Auguste Mariette had the sand, rubbish and mud-brick houses cleared from its precinct, which showed it to be largely intact. In 1848 the town had about 2,000 inhabitants, whose homes stood around and even on the ancient ruins, and who made earthenware vessels like those found in ancient tombs. The temple drew visitors through the 19th century, among them the Prince of Wales in 1862, and the 20th. Excavation at Tell Edfu has been directed since 2001 by Nadine Moeller.
edict-of-nantes: The edict aimed primarily to end the long-running French Wars of Religion. Thirty-six years earlier Catherine de Médici's Edict of Saint-Germain had granted limited tolerance to the Huguenots, but events overtook it: it was not formally registered until after the Massacre of Vassy on 1 March 1562, which set off the first of the wars. Henry IV had been a Protestant before taking the throne in 1589, and it was widely believed that he converted to Catholicism in 1593 only to secure his position. Restoring royal authority required internal peace, based on limited toleration enforced by the crown.

The edict, signed on 18 April 1598, consisted of four basic texts: a main text of 92 articles, 56 particular, secret articles on Protestant rights and obligations, and two brevets, letters patent holding the military and pastoral clauses. It gave general freedom of conscience to individuals, amnesty and the restoration of their civil rights, including the right to work in any field, even for the state. Protestant worship was limited to specified areas, and Catholicism stayed the established religion.

The brevets granted safe havens, military strongholds such as La Rochelle, for which the king paid 180,000 écus a year, and a further 150 emergency forts maintained at Huguenot expense. Pope Clement VIII is reported to have protested on hearing of the edict, This crucifies me. The Parlement of Paris delayed ten months before registering it, in 1599, and the Parlement of Rouen registered it without reservation only in 1609.

The edict restored peace and unity but pleased neither side. Catholics rejected the apparent recognition of Protestantism as a permanent element of French society, and Protestants wanted full parity, which it did not give. In 1629 Louis XIII withdrew the brevets after the siege of La Rochelle, which Cardinal Richelieu blockaded for fourteen months.

In October 1685 Louis XIV, Henry's grandson, revoked the edict with the Edict of Fontainebleau and declared Protestantism illegal. Persecution drove as many as 400,000 people to flee, most to Great Britain, Prussia, the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, South Africa and the colonies in North America. Civil rights for non-Catholics in France were restored only with the Edict of Versailles, signed by Louis XVI on 7 November 1787.
edinburgh: Edinburgh lies in Scotland's Central Belt on the southern shore of the Firth of Forth, between the firth to the north and the Pentland Hills to the south. The modern city is often said to be built on seven hills, among them Calton Hill, Arthur's Seat and the Castle Rock, which gave rise to comparisons with Rome. Castle Rock is a volcanic plug, and the crag and the hollows around it formed an ideal natural strongpoint on which Edinburgh Castle was built. The nickname Auld Reekie, Scots for Old Smoky, refers to the smoke over the Old Town.

The earliest known human habitation in the area was at Cramond, where a Mesolithic camp site dates to about 8500 BCE. The name comes from Eidyn, the name of the region in Cumbric, a Brittonic Celtic language, centred on the stronghold of Din Eidyn, believed to have stood on Castle Rock. A siege of Din Eidyn by Oswald, king of the Angles of Northumbria, in 638 began three centuries of Germanic influence in south-east Scotland, and the town was subsumed in 954 by the kingdom the English called Scotland. As Cumbric gave way to Northumbrian Old English and then Scots, din was replaced by burh, producing Edinburgh.

In 1603 James VI of Scotland succeeded to the English throne, and in 1650 Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army occupied the city. The Acts of Union of 1706 and 1707 united the two kingdoms as Great Britain from 1 May 1707, and the Parliament of Scotland merged into that of Great Britain at Westminster. Many Scots opposed the Union, and there were riots in the city.

The population rose from 49,000 in 1751 to 136,000 in 1831, mostly by migration from the countryside. Overcrowding in the Old Town's tenements and poor sanitation brought cholera outbreaks in 1832, 1848 and 1866. Glasgow overtook Edinburgh as Scotland's largest city by 1821. Improvements under Lord Provost William Chambers in the 1860s began to transform the Old Town, and major slum clearance followed in the 1960s and 1970s.

Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland and one of its 32 council areas, recognised as the capital since at least the 15th century. It is the seat of the Scottish Parliament and Government and of the highest courts in Scotland. The Palace of Holyroodhouse is the monarch's official residence in Scotland. The Old Town and the New Town together are a World Heritage Site, and the University of Edinburgh was founded in 1582.
edirne: Edirne lies in the northwestern part of the province of Edirne in Eastern Thrace, 7 km from the Greek border and 20 km from the Bulgarian border. Its position in the border region between Asia and Europe gave rise to the claim that it is the most frequently contested spot on earth. The through highway that connects Europe to Istanbul, Anatolia and the Middle East passes through it, and the surrounding lowlands are productive farmland.

The city was founded on an earlier Thracian settlement. A Greek city, Orestias, stood on the site, and the Roman emperor Hadrian re-established it, adorned it with monuments and renamed it Hadrianopolis, anglicised as Adrianople. Constantine I defeated Licinius there in 324, and the Emperor Valens was killed by the Goths at the Battle of Adrianople in 378. After the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Versinikia in 813, Khan Krum of Bulgaria seized the city and moved its inhabitants to the Bulgarian lands north of the Danube. In 1077 Nikephoros Bryennios rebelled there against Emperor Michael VII Doukas.

In the period of the Latin Empire of Constantinople, the Bulgarian Emperor Kaloyan defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Adrianople in 1205. The Latin regime gave the city to the Byzantine aristocrat Theodore Branas as a hereditary fief in 1206, and Theodore Komnenos, Despot of Epirus, took it in 1227. In 1321 Andronikos III made it his base for the First Palaiologan civil war against his grandfather, Emperor Andronikos II.

The city fell to the Ottomans around 1369. Its church declined, its properties were confiscated and its Metropolitan was taken prisoner and died in captivity. A document of 1389 states that the new Metropolitan could not enter the city and had to carry out his duties from Constantinople. Edirne was the second capital of the Ottoman Empire from the 1360s to 1453.

Edirne is the seat of Edirne Province and a commercial centre for woven textiles, silks, carpets and agricultural products. The Selimiye Mosque, built in 1575 to the design of Mimar Sinan for Sultan Selim II, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011. Two earlier mosques also stand in the centre: the Eski Cami, begun in 1403 and finished in 1422, and the Üç Şerefli Mosque, built between 1437 and 1447 for Sultan Murad II. The Kırkpınar oil-wrestling tournament, held each year in late June or early July, was inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2010.
edmund-barton: Edmund Barton was born on 18 January 1849 in Glebe, Sydney, the eleventh of twelve children of English parents, William and Mary Louisa Barton, who had arrived in New South Wales in 1827. His father worked as an accountant, stockbroker and estate agent and was once bankrupt; his mother ran a boarding school for girls in hard times. Barton attended Sydney Grammar School, where he was dux and school captain in 1863 and 1864, and matriculated at the University of Sydney in 1865. He was a member of the Sydney University Cricket Club and a founder of the Sydney Rowing Club, and married Jane Mason Ross in 1877.

After losing a university seat in 1876, Barton won a by-election to the New South Wales Legislative Assembly in 1879. In 1882, aged 33, he became Speaker, the youngest presiding officer of any Australian legislative chamber. He entered the Legislative Council in 1887 and served as Attorney General in 1889. An early supporter of federation, he was a delegate to the National Australasian Convention of March 1891 and helped to produce a draft constitution substantially similar to the one enacted in 1900. After the fall of Henry Parkes's government in October 1891, Parkes persuaded him to lead the federal movement in New South Wales.

In 1897 Barton topped the poll of New South Wales delegates to the Constitutional Convention. Sir Samuel Griffith wrote most of the text of the constitution, but Barton was the political leader who carried it through, and he led the campaign for a yes vote in the referendum. He became prime minister on 1 January 1901, the day federation took effect. His ministry was described as a 'cabinet of kings', and after the March 1901 election he stayed in office with the support of the Australian Labor Party. His government set up the Australian Defence Force and the Commonwealth Public Service, introduced nation-wide women's suffrage, and passed the Immigration Restriction Act 1901. In November 1901 Parliament approved Australian control of British New Guinea.

Barton resigned on 24 September 1903 and was sworn in to the High Court on 7 October with Samuel Griffith and Richard O'Connor. On the court he joined Griffith in almost every case and delivered only twelve separate judgments in the 44 cases heard in 1904 and 1905. In 1919 he was disappointed to be passed over as Chief Justice on Griffith's retirement. He died of heart failure on 7 January 1920 at Medlow Bath, New South Wales, and was survived by his wife and six children.
edo-period: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu prevailed at the Battle of Sekigahara and established hegemony over most of Japan, and in 1603 Emperor Go-Yōzei gave him the title of shogun. He had profited from his transfer to the rich Kantō area, where he made Edo, a strategically situated castle town and the future Tokyo, his headquarters. He resigned two years later in favour of his son Hidetada but kept his power, and in 1615 he defeated his main rival, Toyotomi Hideyori, at the Siege of Osaka. He died in 1616. Peace generally prevailed from then on, which made the samurai largely redundant.

The political system is called bakuhan, a joining of bakufu and han, the domains: the shogun held national authority and some 300 daimyo held regional authority. The Tokugawa came to hold nearly seven million koku of land and control of the most important cities. In 1635 Shogun Iemitsu made the system of sankin-kōtai compulsory. It required about 260 daimyo to spend alternate years in Edo, while their wives and heirs stayed there permanently as hostages. Social order was rigid and based on inherited position; scholars since about 1995 have argued that peasants, craftsmen and merchants were a classification rather than a ladder of rank.

Foreign contact was curtailed step by step. Japanese vessels were forbidden to travel abroad without certification in 1633, and the Closed Country Edict of 1635 forbade any Japanese to leave. After the Shimabara Rebellion of 1637, which the shogunate blamed on Christian influence, an edict of 1639 expelled the Portuguese. The Dutch were confined from 1636 to the island of Dejima in Nagasaki.

The period passed on a flourishing commercial sector, a well-educated elite, productive agriculture and a national network of roads, among them the five highways of the Gokaidō. Merchants prospered and laid the foundation of the later zaibatsu. By the mid-18th century Edo had more than one million people, probably the biggest city in the world at the time, and Osaka and Kyoto each had more than 400,000. A commoner culture grew in these cities, with kabuki and ukiyo-e, while Neo-Confucianism became the major intellectual development and the dominant legal philosophy by the mid-17th century.

The period ended after Commodore Matthew C. Perry's squadron appeared in Edo Bay in July 1853. The Treaty of Peace and Amity, or Treaty of Kanagawa, of March 1854 opened two ports to American ships. The shogunate modernised its army and navy in its last years, but the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War restored imperial rule in 1868.
edward-elgar: Elgar's father, William Henry Elgar, was raised in Dover and apprenticed to a London music publisher. In 1841 he moved to Worcester, where he worked as a piano tuner and kept a shop selling sheet music and instruments. Edward was the fourth of seven children. His mother, Ann Elgar, had converted to Roman Catholicism shortly before his birth, and he was baptised and brought up in that faith, to his father's disapproval. William Elgar was a violinist of professional standard and organist of St George's Roman Catholic Church, Worcester, from 1846 to 1885.

At 29 Elgar took a pupil, Caroline Alice Roberts, eight years his senior. They married on 8 May 1889 at Brompton Oratory. Her family was horrified, and she was disinherited. She acted as his business manager and social secretary, and their daughter Carice Irene was born on 14 August 1890.

During the 1890s Elgar built a reputation with works for the choral festivals of the English Midlands, among them The Black Knight (1892), King Olaf (1896) and Caractacus (1898), and gained a long-standing publisher in Novello and Co. For the Birmingham Triennial Music Festival of 1900 he set Cardinal John Henry Newman's poem The Dream of Gerontius. Hans Richter conducted the premiere, in which a poorly prepared chorus sang badly. Performances in Düsseldorf in 1901 and 1902 drew an enthusiastic German press, and Richard Strauss proposed a toast to him in his presence.

Some of the Anglican establishment disliked the Catholic text. Charles Villiers Stanford complained that it stank of incense, and the dean of Gloucester banned it from his cathedral in 1901. Elgar was knighted in 1904, appointed to the Order of Merit in June 1911 and created a baronet in 1931. Alice Elgar died of lung cancer on 7 April 1920.

Elgar was contemptuous of folk music. The continental composers who most influenced him were Handel, Dvořák and, to some degree, Brahms, and his orchestration owes much to French composers, above all Delibes.
